h1: Male Pattern Baldness: How Fast, and What Slows It
subtitle: Predictable pattern, variable speed. The earlier you read it, the more you keep.

hero.alt: 200x view of the crown in male pattern thinning
hero.caption: The crown against your control zone, at 200x.

quickAnswer: Male pattern baldness is DHT-driven miniaturization following a predictable distribution: the temples recede, the crown thins, and the back and sides stay dense because those follicles are not androgen-sensitive. Speed varies widely. Some men lose noticeable density in two or three years, others hold a stable pattern for a decade. What determines your pace is inherited follicle sensitivity, which is why family history is useful information. The practical point is that follicles producing fine hair can still be supported, while follicles that stopped producing years ago cannot be argued back. Reading your crown at 200x tells us which stage you are in. Nina Ross Atlanta is in Sandy Springs, serving all of Metro Atlanta.
takeaways: The back and sides are usually spared.
Your pace is inherited, and it varies widely.
Follicles still producing fine hair can be supported.

items.you: My hairline is going back at the corners
items.why: Recession at the corners is commonly linked to DHT-sensitive follicles at the temples producing finer hair each cycle.
items.check: We read the corners at 200x and compare them with the back of your head to measure how far it has moved.

items.you: There is a thin spot at my crown
items.why: A thin spot at the crown is commonly linked to miniaturization, where follicles keep producing finer, shorter hair.
items.check: We photograph the crown at 200x and set a baseline you can measure against at every visit.

items.why: The follicles at the back and sides are not sensitive to DHT, which is why they stay dense while the top thins.
items.check: We use the back as your personal control zone. Comparing it with the crown shows exactly how far the pattern has moved.

items.you: My hair will not grow past a certain length up top
items.why: When hair on top stops growing past a certain length, it is commonly because DHT has shortened the growth phase.
items.check: We read length and thickness at 200x to see how much the cycle has shifted.

items.you: My line is patchy when I get a fade
items.us: Reduced density visible at short lengths
items.why: Short cuts make lower density easier to see, so a patchy line is often the first sign your barber notices.
items.check: We read the hairline at 200x to tell pattern thinning from other causes, like tension or scalp irritation.

items.title: Inherited DHT sensitivity
items.text: The follicles you inherited determine which zones respond to DHT and how quickly they shrink.{cite:1}

items.title: Age and cumulative exposure
items.text: Each growth cycle under DHT pressure produces a slightly finer hair, so the pattern deepens over years rather than months.

items.title: Metabolic and stress load
items.text: Insulin resistance, poor sleep and sustained stress do not cause the pattern, and they can speed up how fast it shows.

faq.q: How fast will I lose it?
faq.a: Nobody can tell you a date. What we can do is measure your current stage at 200x and re-measure it, so your actual pace becomes visible instead of theoretical.

faq.q: Is it too late for me?
faq.a: That depends on how many follicles are still producing hair, even fine hair. Those can be supported. Areas that stopped producing years ago are a different conversation, and we tell you which you have. Results not typical. Individual results will vary.

faq.q: Why does the back never go?
faq.a: The follicles at the back and sides are not sensitive to DHT, so they keep producing full-thickness hair while the top thins.

faq.q: Does wearing a cap or a durag cause this?
faq.a: Male pattern baldness is driven by inherited DHT sensitivity. Tension or friction from anything worn tight is a separate finding, and we read it separately.

faq.q: Do you work with Black men specifically?
faq.a: Yes. We read textured hair every day, including fades, waves and locs, and we know how pattern thinning shows up at short lengths.
